It solves the problem of efficiently computing ray-volume intersections without requiring complex ray-triangle intersection logic in the main rendering pass by rasterizing the volume's bounding box faces into offscreen textures [S3, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly describes a two-pass technique where Pass 1 involves rasterizing the volume's bounding box faces into offscreen textures (BackfaceTexture and FrontfaceTexture) using OpenGL FBOs and face culling. Pass 2 then uses these textures to determine ray start and end positions for the raycasting fragment shader. This approach avoids performing complex ray-volume (or ray-triangle) intersection calculations within the main raycasting fragment shader loop, instead relying on the rasterization of the bounding box to define the ray segment. Thus, the claim accurately reflects the method described in Source [S3].
